name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_RESPIRATIONINPLANTS_MCQ_Q01 - Cellular sites and gaseous exchange in plants

questiontext.text:
Evaluate the following four statements regarding respiration and gaseous exchange in plants:

Statement I: In eukaryotes, photosynthesis occurs within chloroplasts, whereas the breakdown of complex molecules to yield energy occurs in the cytoplasm and mitochondria.

Statement II: Plants lack specialised respiratory organs and instead rely on stomata and lenticels for gaseous exchange.

Statement III: Roots, stems, and leaves respire at rates far lower than animals do.

Statement IV: In thick, woody stems, living cells are organised in thin layers inside and beneath the bark, while cells in the interior are dead and provide mechanical support.

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Cellular respiration in plants is compartmentalised between the cytoplasm and mitochondria, and plants manage gaseous exchange without specialised respiratory organs due to low metabolic demand and favourable cellular arrangement.

Step 2: Evaluation of Subcellular Sites and Exchange Structures
In eukaryotic plant cells, photosynthesis is restricted to chloroplasts, while respiratory breakdown of food molecules takes place in the cytoplasm (glycolysis) and mitochondria (aerobic oxidation). For gas exchange, plants lack lungs or gills and instead use stomata and lenticels.

Step 3: Evaluation of Respiration Rates and Woody Stem Anatomy
Plant organs such as roots, stems, and leaves exhibit much lower respiration rates than animal tissues, so they do not require rapid bulk transport of gases. In thick, woody stems, living cells are arranged in thin layers inside and beneath the bark near lenticels, whereas interior cells are dead and function solely in mechanical support.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
All four propositions—concerning the cytoplasmic and mitochondrial sites of respiration, the use of stomata and lenticels, the lower respiration rates in plant organs, and the peripheral arrangement of living cells in woody stems—are correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_RESPIRATIONINPLANTS_MCQ_Q02 - Pathway and enzymatic requirements of glycolysis

questiontext.text:
Evaluate the following four statements regarding glycolysis:

Statement I: The scheme of glycolysis, often called the EMP pathway, occurs in the cytoplasm of all living organisms.

Statement II: In plants, sucrose is converted into glucose and fructose by the enzyme invertase before entering glycolysis.

Statement III: Glucose and fructose are phosphorylated to form glucose-6-phosphate by the enzyme hexokinase.

Statement IV: Molecular oxygen is directly required for the conversion of glucose to two molecules of pyruvic acid.

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Glycolysis (the Embden–Meyerhof–Parnas or EMP pathway) is the universal cytosolic pathway that partially oxidises glucose into two molecules of pyruvic acid.

Step 2: Evaluation of Location and Initial Enzymatic Steps
Glycolysis takes place in the cytoplasm of all living organisms. In plants, sucrose (the end product of photosynthesis) is hydrolysed into glucose and fructose by invertase, and these monosaccharides are phosphorylated by hexokinase to give rise to glucose-6-phosphate, which enters the subsequent glycolytic reactions.

Step 3: Evaluation of Oxygen Requirement
Glycolysis is an anaerobic process that partially oxidises glucose without the participation of molecular oxygen; therefore, claiming that \(\text{O}_2\) is directly required for converting glucose to pyruvic acid is incorrect.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The propositions describing the cytoplasmic EMP pathway, sucrose cleavage by invertase, and phosphorylation by hexokinase are correct, whereas the proposition claiming a direct requirement for molecular oxygen in glycolysis is incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_RESPIRATIONINPLANTS_MCQ_Q03 - Energy investment and payoff in glycolysis

questiontext.text:
Evaluate the following four statements regarding the steps of glycolysis per molecule of glucose:

Statement I: \(\text{ATP}\) is utilised in the conversion of glucose to glucose-6-phosphate and fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate.

Statement II: Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate is split into dihydroxyacetone phosphate and 3-phosphoglyceraldehyde (\(\text{PGAL}\)).

Statement III: \(\text{NADH} + \text{H}^+\) is formed from \(\text{NAD}^+\) during the conversion of 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate (\(\text{BPGA}\)) to 3-phosphoglyceric acid (\(\text{PGA}\)).

Statement IV: A total of 4 \(\text{ATP}\) molecules are directly synthesised during glycolysis from one molecule of glucose.

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Glycolysis involves a preparatory phase that consumes \(\text{ATP}\) and splits a 6-carbon sugar bisphosphate into two 3-carbon triose phosphates, followed by a payoff phase that generates \(\text{NADH} + \text{H}^+\) and \(\text{ATP}\).

Step 2: Evaluation of Investment and Splitting Steps
Two \(\text{ATP}\) molecules are consumed per glucose: one in converting glucose to glucose-6-phosphate and one in converting fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate. Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate then splits into dihydroxyacetone phosphate and 3-phosphoglyceraldehyde (\(\text{PGAL}\)).

Step 3: Evaluation of Redox and Direct ATP Synthesis
\(\text{NADH} + \text{H}^+\) is generated when \(\text{PGAL}\) is oxidised and phosphorylated to 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate (\(\text{BPGA}\)), not during the conversion of \(\text{BPGA}\) to \(\text{PGA}\) (which instead generates \(\text{ATP}\)). Because each 6-carbon glucose yields two 3-carbon triose phosphates, direct \(\text{ATP}\) synthesis occurs twice at \(\text{BPGA} \rightarrow \text{PGA}\) (\(2\text{ ATP}\)) and twice at \(\text{PEP} \rightarrow \text{pyruvic acid}\) (\(2\text{ ATP}\)), giving \(4\text{ ATP}\) directly synthesised.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The propositions regarding the two \(\text{ATP}\)-consuming steps, the splitting of fructose-1,6-bisphosphate, and the direct synthesis of 4 \(\text{ATP}\) molecules per glucose are correct, whereas the proposition placing \(\text{NADH} + \text{H}^+\) formation at the \(\text{BPGA}\) to \(\text{PGA}\) step is incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_RESPIRATIONINPLANTS_MCQ_Q04 - Pathways, enzymes, and limits of fermentation

questiontext.text:
Evaluate the following four statements regarding anaerobic fermentation:

Statement I: In yeast, pyruvic acid is converted to \(\text{CO}_2\) and ethanol by pyruvic acid decarboxylase and alcohol dehydrogenase.

Statement II: In animal muscle cells during intense exercise when oxygen is inadequate, pyruvic acid is converted to ethanol and \(\text{CO}_2\).

Statement III: In both lactic acid fermentation and alcoholic fermentation, \(\text{NADH} + \text{H}^+\) is reoxidised to \(\text{NAD}^+\).

Statement IV: Less than 7 per cent of the energy in glucose is released during fermentation, and yeasts poison themselves to death when alcohol concentration reaches about 13 per cent.

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Fermentation represents the incomplete anaerobic oxidation of glucose in which pyruvate is reduced to regenerate \(\text{NAD}^+\), yielding only a small fraction of the energy stored in glucose.

Step 2: Evaluation of Yeast and Muscle Fermentation
In yeast, pyruvic acid is converted to ethanol and \(\text{CO}_2\) by pyruvic acid decarboxylase and alcohol dehydrogenase. In animal muscles under oxygen-deficient conditions during exercise, however, pyruvic acid is reduced to lactic acid by lactate dehydrogenase—not to ethanol and \(\text{CO}_2\).

Step 3: Evaluation of Redox Regeneration and Energy/Toxicity Limits
Both fermentation pathways use \(\text{NADH} + \text{H}^+\) as the reducing agent, reoxidising it to \(\text{NAD}^+\) to sustain glycolysis. In both pathways, less than 7 per cent of the energy in glucose is released, and yeasts poison themselves to death when alcohol concentration reaches about 13 per cent.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The propositions concerning yeast fermentation enzymes, reoxidation of \(\text{NADH} + \text{H}^+\) to \(\text{NAD}^+\), and the 7 per cent energy release limit with 13 per cent alcohol toxicity are correct, whereas the proposition claiming ethanol and \(\text{CO}_2\) formation in exercising animal muscles is incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_RESPIRATIONINPLANTS_MCQ_Q05 - Link reaction and tricarboxylic acid cycle

questiontext.text:
Evaluate the following four statements regarding aerobic oxidation of pyruvate in eukaryotes:

Statement I: Oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvic acid to acetyl \(\text{CoA}\) by pyruvate dehydrogenase occurs in the cytoplasm before pyruvate enters the mitochondrion.

Statement II: The TCA cycle begins with the condensation of the acetyl group with oxaloacetic acid (\(\text{OAA}\)) and water to yield citric acid, catalysed by citrate synthase.

Statement III: Isomerisation of citrate to isocitrate is followed by two successive decarboxylation steps leading to \(\alpha\)-ketoglutaric acid and then succinyl-\(\text{CoA}\).

Statement IV: Conversion of succinyl-\(\text{CoA}\) to succinic acid synthesises \(\text{GTP}\) by substrate-level phosphorylation, which is coupled to \(\text{ATP}\) synthesis from \(\text{ADP}\).

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In aerobic respiration, pyruvate is transported from the cytosol into the mitochondrial matrix, where it is converted into acetyl \(\text{CoA}\) and oxidised via the tricarboxylic acid (Krebs') cycle.

Step 2: Evaluation of Site of Pyruvate Dehydrogenation
Pyruvate is transported into the mitochondrial matrix first, and only there undergoes oxidative decarboxylation catalysed by pyruvate dehydrogenase in the presence of \(\text{Mg}^{2+}\), \(\text{NAD}^+\), and \(\text{CoA}\). Therefore, claiming this reaction occurs in the cytoplasm is incorrect.

Step 3: Evaluation of TCA Cycle Reactions
Within the mitochondrial matrix, citrate synthase catalyses the condensation of the acetyl group with oxaloacetic acid and water to form citric acid. Citrate isomerises to isocitrate, followed by two successive decarboxylations yielding \(\alpha\)-ketoglutaric acid and then succinyl-\(\text{CoA}\). Subsequently, conversion of succinyl-\(\text{CoA}\) to succinic acid generates \(\text{GTP}\) via substrate-level phosphorylation, coupled to \(\text{ATP}\) formation from \(\text{ADP}\).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The propositions describing citrate synthase initiation, the two successive decarboxylations to \(\alpha\)-ketoglutaric acid and succinyl-\(\text{CoA}\), and \(\text{GTP}\)-coupled substrate-level phosphorylation are correct, whereas the proposition placing pyruvate dehydrogenase activity in the cytoplasm is incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_RESPIRATIONINPLANTS_MCQ_Q06 - Electron carriers and complexes of the mitochondrial ETS

questiontext.text:
Evaluate the following four statements regarding the mitochondrial Electron Transport System (ETS):

Statement I: Electrons from \(\text{NADH}\) produced in the mitochondrial matrix are oxidised by \(\text{NADH}\) dehydrogenase (Complex I) and transferred to ubiquinone.

Statement II: Ubiquinone also receives reducing equivalents via \(\text{FADH}_2\) (Complex II) generated during the oxidation of succinate in the citric acid cycle.

Statement III: Cytochrome \(c\) is an integral membrane protein complex located between Complex I and Complex II within the inner mitochondrial membrane.

Statement IV: Complex IV is the cytochrome \(c\) oxidase complex containing cytochromes \(a\) and \(a_3\) and two copper centres.

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The electron transport system (ETS) on the inner mitochondrial membrane channels electrons from \(\text{NADH}\) and \(\text{FADH}_2\) through Complexes I–IV to molecular oxygen.

Step 2: Evaluation of Complexes I, II, and IV
Complex I (\(\text{NADH}\) dehydrogenase) oxidises matrix \(\text{NADH}\) and transfers electrons to ubiquinone. Ubiquinone also accepts reducing equivalents from \(\text{FADH}_2\) via Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) during succinate oxidation. Complex IV is the cytochrome \(c\) oxidase complex, which contains cytochromes \(a\) and \(a_3\) along with two copper centres.

Step 3: Evaluation of Cytochrome c
Cytochrome \(c\) is a small protein attached to the outer surface of the inner mitochondrial membrane—not an integral membrane complex—and it acts as a mobile carrier transferring electrons between Complex III (cytochrome \(bc_1\)) and Complex IV, not between Complex I and Complex II.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The propositions regarding Complex I electron transfer to ubiquinone, Complex II \(\text{FADH}_2\) entry to ubiquinone, and the composition of Complex IV are correct, whereas the proposition describing cytochrome \(c\) as an integral membrane complex between Complex I and Complex II is incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_RESPIRATIONINPLANTS_MCQ_Q07 - Oxidative phosphorylation and respiratory balance sheet

questiontext.text:
Evaluate the following four statements regarding oxidative phosphorylation and the respiratory balance sheet:

Statement I: Oxidation of one molecule of \(\text{NADH}\) through the ETS yields 3 molecules of \(\text{ATP}\), whereas oxidation of one molecule of \(\text{FADH}_2\) produces 2 molecules of \(\text{ATP}\).

Statement II: For each \(\text{ATP}\) synthesised by \(\text{ATP}\) synthase (Complex V), \(2\text{H}^+\) passes through the \(\text{F}_0\) channel from the intermembrane space to the mitochondrial matrix.

Statement III: The theoretical net gain of 38 \(\text{ATP}\) molecules per glucose assumes that glycolytic \(\text{NADH}\) is transferred into the mitochondria and undergoes oxidative phosphorylation.

Statement IV: In living cells, glycolysis, the TCA cycle, and the ETS operate strictly sequentially one after another without any intermediates being withdrawn.

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Membrane-linked \(\text{ATP}\) synthesis in mitochondria relies on an electrochemical proton gradient across the inner membrane, and the 38 \(\text{ATP}\) respiratory balance sheet is an idealised theoretical calculation.

Step 2: Evaluation of ATP Yields and Proton Channel Stoichiometry
In the ETS, oxidation of one \(\text{NADH}\) yields 3 \(\text{ATP}\), while oxidation of one \(\text{FADH}_2\) yields 2 \(\text{ATP}\). At Complex V (\(\text{ATP}\) synthase), \(2\text{H}^+\) flows through the integral \(\text{F}_0\) channel from the intermembrane space to the matrix down the electrochemical gradient for each \(\text{ATP}\) synthesised at the \(\text{F}_1\) headpiece.

Step 3: Evaluation of Balance Sheet Assumptions vs Living Reality
Calculating a net gain of 38 \(\text{ATP}\) per glucose requires assuming that glycolytic \(\text{NADH}\) enters mitochondria for oxidative phosphorylation, that pathways run sequentially, and that no intermediates are withdrawn. However, in actual living systems, all pathways operate simultaneously rather than sequentially, and substrates enter and are withdrawn as needed.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The propositions regarding \(\text{NADH}\)/\(\text{FADH}_2\) \(\text{ATP}\) yields, \(2\text{H}^+\) passage per \(\text{ATP}\) through \(\text{F}_0\), and the mitochondrial-transfer assumption for 38 \(\text{ATP}\) are correct, whereas the proposition claiming strictly sequential, isolated operation in living cells is incorrect.

questiontext.text:
Evaluate the following four statements regarding the amphibolic pathway and respiratory quotient (\(\text{RQ}\)):

Statement I: When fats are respired, fatty acids are degraded to acetyl \(\text{CoA}\) and glycerol is converted to \(\text{PGAL}\) before entering the respiratory pathway.

Statement II: Deaminated amino acids always enter the respiratory pathway exclusively as glucose-6-phosphate.

Statement III: Because intermediates such as acetyl \(\text{CoA}\) are both fed into the pathway during breakdown and withdrawn for synthesis of biomolecules, the respiratory pathway is amphibolic.

Statement IV: For complete oxidation of tripalmitin, \(\text{RQ} = \frac{102\text{CO}_2}{145\text{O}_2} = 0.7\), and in living organisms pure proteins or fats are never used as sole respiratory substrates.

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Non-carbohydrate substrates enter the respiratory pathway at specific intermediate points, the pathway supplies intermediates for anabolism as well as catabolism (making it amphibolic), and the respiratory quotient (\(\text{RQ}\)) reflects the chemical nature of the substrate oxidised.

Step 2: Evaluation of Fat and Protein Entry and Amphibolic Role
Fatty acids are degraded to acetyl \(\text{CoA}\) and glycerol is converted to \(\text{PGAL}\) to enter respiration. In contrast, amino acids (after deamination) enter at some stage within the Krebs' cycle or as pyruvate or acetyl \(\text{CoA}\)—not exclusively as glucose-6-phosphate. Because compounds like acetyl \(\text{CoA}\) are also withdrawn for fatty acid synthesis, the respiratory pathway is amphibolic.

Step 3: Evaluation of Tripalmitin RQ and Mixed Substrates
From the balanced equation \(2(\text{C}_{51}\text{H}_{98}\text{O}_6) + 145\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 102\text{CO}_2 + 98\text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{energy}\), the \(\text{RQ}\) for tripalmitin is \(\frac{102}{145} \approx 0.7\). In living organisms, more than one respiratory substrate is typically used, and pure proteins or fats are never used as sole respiratory substrates.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The propositions describing fat breakdown entry points, the amphibolic nature of respiration, and the \(0.7\) \(\text{RQ}\) of tripalmitin with mixed substrate usage are correct, whereas the proposition claiming deaminated amino acids enter exclusively as glucose-6-phosphate is incorrect.
